intro: The repeated note in the “Raindrop” Prelude survives a change from D♭ major to a darker minor-key setting written C♯ minor. In Ivan Ilić’s recording, follow that persistent sound as its register, surroundings and expressive weight change, then listen for the opening melody’s return.
question: What changes around the repeated note, and what remains recognisable?

sections.label: A′ · Opening song returns
sections.mNote: the opening melody returns after the darker middle

cues.title: A repeated note persists
cues.text: The melody moves above a recurring A♭. Listen to both layers: the repeated pitch supplies continuity while changing harmony and melodic direction keep the passage from standing still.
cues.evidence: Repeated-note construction: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/208; pitch identity and tonal plan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude,_Op._28,_No._15_(Chopin).

cues.title: Winter at Valldemossa
cues.text: Chopin completed the collection during the Mallorca winter of 1838–39 with George Sand and her children. The difficult weather belongs to that history, but it does not require the music to imitate a storm.
cues.evidence: Mallorca completion in https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/gatunki/12_preludia; Sand’s weather account and Chopin’s rejection of literal imitation in https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/208

cues.title: A memoir, not a programme
cues.text: Sand associated Chopin’s music with falling rain and recalled his resistance to literal imitation. The familiar nickname can be a starting point for attention, but a repeated note also has a musical function independent of that story.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski discusses Sand’s memoir and the disputed relation between imitation and musical association: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/208. No claim that the anecdote proves a literal programme.

cues.title: The same pitch changes setting
cues.text: The middle turns to C♯ minor and a darker register. The recurring A♭ is respelled G♯: the sounding pitch remains, but its harmonic and registral surroundings give it a different weight.
cues.evidence: Approximate boundary at1:26, where the report marks a change in density and colour. Written enharmonic pitch and tonal plan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude,_Op._28,_No._15_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A longer dynamic rise
cues.text: The middle has more than one wave of intensity. Listen across the whole phrase rather than treating each louder chord as the ultimate crest; the repeated note continues beneath the changing pressure.
cues.evidence: Report shows a crest around1:55–2:00, a retreat near2:05, and a later stronger rise around2:35–2:40. These are broad amplitude contours, not exact written dynamic markings.

cues.title: Bach and a different order
cues.text: Chopin had Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier with him in Mallorca. Both collections cover all major and minor keys, but Chopin orders his preludes in major–relative-minor pairs around the circle of fifths, not Bach’s chromatic sequence.

cues.title: Persistence inside changing weight
cues.text: In the later middle, compare the continuing repeated pitch with the phrases around it. A persistent note can sound like support, insistence or a point of resistance depending on register, harmony and dynamics.
cues.evidence: Listening invitation within the C♯-minor middle; no single instantaneous emotional or harmonic event is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening song returns
cues.text: The D♭-major melody returns after the darker central span. Its earlier character becomes recognisable again, but the return is shorter: Chopin does not repeat the entire opening at its original length.
cues.evidence: Approximate return around3:30 after a broad withdrawal in the3:20–3:30 windows. ABA return and shortened reprise: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude,_Op._28,_No._15_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hear the ending’s space
cues.text: The last phrases let the sound recede rather than repeating the middle’s weight. Listen to the gaps between gestures and to the surviving melodic contour as the piece comes to rest.
cues.evidence: Report boundaries at4:04 and declining late activity place this cue in the closing span. No particular pedal release or exact final-note onset is asserted.

transitions.title: A persistent pitch enters a darker setting
transitions.how: The opening melody yields to the middle’s lower, darker texture. D♭ major becomes C♯ minor in the notation, while the recurring A♭ is respelled G♯. The shared sounding pitch acts as a link, but new harmony, register and chordal weight change what that continuity feels like.
transitions.evidence: Approximate1:26 report boundary. Written keys and recurring pitch: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude,_Op._28,_No._15_(Chopin); the chroma estimate is not the harmonic source.

transitions.title: The repeated pitch leads back to the song
transitions.how: The middle’s accumulated force recedes and the D♭-major opening melody returns. The recurring pitch links the two tonal spellings, while the lighter texture and recovered melodic contour make the reprise recognisable. The return is abbreviated, directing the music towards its close rather than beginning the whole argument again.
transitions.evidence: Approximate return around3:30 follows lower-level3:20–3:30 windows. Tonal plan and shortened reprise: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prelude,_Op._28,_No._15_(Chopin).

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
